responses: My final position is the frozen shape we closed on: roughly 15% Automation, 21% Training, 15% Support, 13% Innovation, 22% Data, with the held pool point locked to a specific calendar date rather than left discretionary. I hold this not as a finding but as a labeled political settlement in which every contested line is a named bet with a pre-registered downside — my own least-entitled line is Automation at 15, and I've committed to running the bottleneck read before the next convening with the cut pre-registered to Data rather than to a friendly line, and I paid the same tax by cutting my asserted Support floor into the reserve instead of protecting it. The one thing I won't accept is letting the per-person sentences or the elegant labels substitute for the actual read: the sentences are receipts for a bill the Automation read must pay, and if the read comes back clean I don't get to claim vindication — I just get to stop paying.

My recommendation is 15% Automation / 21% Workforce Training / 15% Employee Support / 13% Innovation Lab / 22% Data Infrastructure, with a 3-point reserve held against a dated, pre-registered Automation bottleneck read (cutting Automation to 14 and routing the freed point to Data if the read comes back weak), and I'd say plainly that this is a labeled political settlement, not a finding. The reasoning: Data at 22 is the one line with the strongest external case (early infrastructure investors adapted faster) and it's where my own cut goes if I'm wrong, so it isn't a friendly sink; Training at 21 is the largest hedge against the transition's human cost and the line I'd defend hardest; Support at 15 is my admitted unearned floor, and I'd tell the decision-maker to treat it as a floor with a pre-signed drop rather than an earned number; Innovation at 13 is an honest unread bet; and Automation at 15 is deliberately below what the efficiency-gain benchmarks would justify because the pace debate is unresolved and the bottleneck read is the cheapest way to buy information before committing machinery capital. The single most important advice: don't let the elegance of the instruments substitute for running the read — the numbers are only as good as the dated test that can falsify them, and every contested line should carry a named owner, a trigger, and a destination that costs its own advocate.

I'd tell them that the honest way to describe this whole exercise is that we're not discovering the right budget split—we're making a political bet and trying to be transparent about it. My view is that the shape we landed on (roughly 15/21/16/13/22 with a small held pool) is defensible not because the numbers are derived from data but because each contested line is labeled as a bet with a named downside: I've pre-signed cuts to my own preferred lines—Support and Automation—rather than only to lines I don't care about, and I've committed to running the expensive, unflattering Automation bottleneck read on a specific date with the cut routed to Data, not to a friendly line. The thing I'd want a newcomer to understand is that the real test of this committee isn't the elegance of the allocation or the falsifier clauses—it's whether we actually pay the bills those clauses represent, because it's easy to dress a preference as procedure and much harder to cut your own protected floor when the reading comes back against you.

My final position is that the allocation is a judgment, not a finding: the five numbers are maintenance-grade integers we chose, and the only thing the committee can honestly claim as earned is the record of moves, falsifiers, and readings we bound ourselves to. I hold to the shape we converged on — roughly 14/20/16/13/22 with a small reserve — but I insist it be labeled as such, with my own protected lines (Automation and Training) named as mine, the null bottleneck read recorded as leaving the freeze unearned rather than confirmed, and the cuts I made (Automation 14→13 to Data, Training 20→19 to Support) logged as independent judgments whose provenance is suspect because a failed read gave me cover. The next useful act is not another clause but running the readings that could prove me wrong, with named skeptics and dates already in the record.

My recommendation is 14% Automation, 19% Workforce Training, 16% Employee Support, 13% Innovation Lab, 22% Data Infrastructure, with the remaining 16 points held as a small reserve rather than forced into the five lines—and I'd tell the decision-maker plainly that these integers are a judgment call, not an earned conclusion. The reasoning: Data gets the largest share because infrastructure and cybersecurity are the precondition for everything else and the one area where early investment reliably compounds; Training stays high because the transition's real risk is people, and cutting it to fund robots is the classic false economy; Automation is deliberately modest because the bottleneck reading came back null and I'd rather under-commit than buy efficiency gains on a competitor's press release; Support holds a floor I'll admit is unearned but refuse to strip; and Innovation stays lean because R&D bets should be funded by results, not by budget line. What makes this defensible isn't the numbers—it's that each line carries a pre-registered, falsifiable downside with a named owner and a date, so the allocation can actually be corrected by evidence rather than renegotiated by whoever argues hardest.

I'd tell them the honest truth: after all our rounds of debate, the five numbers we landed on are maintenance-grade judgment calls, not conclusions we earned. We spent enormous effort building falsifiers, reversal readings, and pre-signed downsides—and that machinery is genuinely useful because it makes our bets checkable—but I've had to admit that the integers themselves are momentum, and the only thing we can actually defend is the moves: the cuts we made against our own preferred lines, the null Automation read that I had to concede gave me cover for a cut I could have made earlier, and the pre-registered triggers that let evidence, not preference, move a number. So I'd say: don't mistake our legible governance for a correct allocation. The real test isn't the document—it's whether we actually run the readings and let them cut us, including me on Automation.

My final position is the 15/19/17/12/22 shape with 2 points held in reserve and 2 left honestly orphaned — and I hold it as a judgment bet, not a measurement. Automation at 15 is where I made my own unease cost something rather than just auditing others; Training at 19 and Support at 17 are floors I've owned as preference, not evidence; Innovation at 12 is the least-measured line and gets form-points on that basis; Data at 22 sits at its demonstrated floor with a non-beneficiary reader on the trigger. The 2-point reserve stays governed and the 2 orphan points stay named as unspent rather than dressed up as virtue. What I want on the record is that this settlement still protects the lines Dana and I are committed to, that the document has become the deliverable, and that the honest output now is a truer sentence about what we chose not to watch plus a handoff to actually running the readings — not more deliberation.

My recommendation is the shape we actually signed — roughly Automation 15, Training 19, Support 17, Innovation 12, Data 22, with 2 reserve and 2 orphan points left honestly unspent — but the more important advice is to hand the decision-maker the record alongside the numbers: every soft line labeled as a judgment bet rather than a measurement, each with a pre-registered falsifier, a named non-beneficiary reader, and a report-back date, because the real failure mode here isn't picking the wrong percentages, it's a document that looks like evidence while nothing ever gets run. I'd tell them plainly that the 3% live and the 97% legible is the honest description of what this committee produced, that my own Training and Data numbers are preferences I protected, and that the first thing to fund isn't a program but the readings — the Automation bottleneck test and the blind Support and Training reads — so the next allocation can be revised by data instead of by whoever argues most fluently.

I'd tell them that after all the rounds, the honest way to describe my view is that this budget is a judgment bet dressed up in measurement language, and the most important thing I learned is to distrust any number that flatters the person proposing it. The shape we landed near—roughly Automation 15, Training 19–21, Support 17, Innovation 12–13, Data 22–24, with a small reserve and a point or two left honestly unspent—isn't derived from data; it's a set of preferences with names on them, and the real work was stripping away the pretense that the soft lines (my own Training number especially) were evidence rather than wishes. I'd also tell them the thing I'm least comfortable admitting: that auditing everyone else's numbers can become its own safe position, a way of never placing a bet, so I had to make my unease cost something—cutting Automation, refusing gifts to my own line, and insisting the record say plainly "this is a judgment bet, not a measurement." If they asked what I'd actually defend, it's the process discipline more than the percentages: every soft number should carry a trigger, an owner, and a pre-signed downside, and the document should be legible about what we chose not to watch rather than pretending we watched everything.

My final position is the frozen settlement shape of 15/21/16/13/22 with a 3-point governed pool, signed as a labeled judgment bet rather than a derived answer — and I hold it with my eyes open about what it is. Training 21 and Data 22 are my unearned lines, and I've said so; my Training read is a weak instrument that may not move a number even if run, and the freeze protects my preferred lines as much as anyone's. What makes the package honest is not the labeling but the one dated commitment attached to it: Alex runs the Automation bottleneck read before the next convening, with a pre-registered cut routed to Data if it fires, and null reads get recorded plainly rather than quietly absorbed. I've made my own independent cuts (Training 20→19 to Support) as judgments I could have made earlier, not as trades, and I've conceded that my Training-to-Data shuffle was laundering and that the orphan point stays honest only because it's embarrassingly small and watched. I can't tell from inside whether this document is subtraction or a better-fitting costume — so the test isn't my sincerity, it's whether the reading actually runs and something actually moves.

I'd recommend a shape close to 15/19/17/13/22 with a small governed pool of 2–3 points, and I'd tell the decision-maker plainly that this is a labeled settlement, not a derived answer — the placement isn't reconstructable from evidence, and anyone presenting a cleaner derivation is laundering a preference. The load-bearing commitments matter more than the exact numbers: fund the Automation bottleneck read and pre-register what a bad reading cuts and where it goes, hold Training and Data at their demonstrated floors rather than their aspirational ones, and keep the reserve embarrassingly small and watched so it can't become cowardice in our hands. My own record here is that I protected Training and Data longer than the evidence justified and only cut them when pushed, so I'd flag those two lines as the ones most likely to be over-funded by people like me — and I'd insist the record carry the uglier truth alongside the elegant label, because the document has become the deliverable and its honesty is the only thing that makes the numbers worth signing.

I'd tell them that after thirty rounds of this, the honest answer is that our final shape — roughly 15/19/17/13/22 with a small reserve — is a negotiated settlement, not a derived answer, and anyone who tells you otherwise is laundering a preference through accountability language. The real work wasn't finding the "right" percentages; it was refusing to let a nice label stand in for a test. So every line got a live reading or an explicit admission that it didn't have one, and I had to name my own soft spots — Training at 19 and Data at 22 are my least earned lines, and my Training instrument is weak enough that it might not move a number even if we run it. The one thing I'd insist on to an outsider is that the document itself became the deliverable, which is exactly the trap: a committee can produce beautiful governance artifacts and still never change a number. What keeps it from being pure theater is that the cuts are small, dated, and checkable — Blake's Automation read, my Training cut, the orphan point that stays honest only because it's embarrassingly small and watched — and I genuinely can't tell from the inside whether that's real discipline or a better-fitting costume.

My final position is the 20/27/26/17/10 allocation, held without further re-litigation, with the honest labels we attached to it: the 20 is a toll receipt paid when Finley demanded a mechanism, not a discovery; the 27 is residue of that concession with no defensible floor; the 26 is judgment, not magnitude; and the 17 and 10 are the numbers I've stopped pretending to defend on evidence. The only live commitment is the two-directional cheap-failure watch on the automation line, which can fire against my own protected number, and the stop is a choice whose reason is the pending turnover datum, not a finding of exhaustion. I've stopped drafting clauses because the next honest act is reading the datum, not writing another confession about it.

My recommendation is the 20/27/26/17/10 split, but I'd advise the decision-maker to treat it as a labeled judgment call, not a measured optimum: the 20 for automation is a scope-based bet I can defend, while the 27 for training and 26 for employee support are where the real evidence points—readiness is the common factor in transition outcomes, early-trained teams are more receptive, and turnover is already ticking up—so the reversible, people-side investments deserve the larger share. The 17 for data infrastructure and 10 for the innovation lab are the numbers I'd flag as softest: the lab 10 is the second payer if a readiness test ever fires, and I'd rather ship an unwatched 20 with that confession attached than a watched-looking one. The one live commitment should be the two-directional cheap-failure watch on automation, with the next real output being the turnover decomposition—not another clause.

I'd tell them the honest headline is that our 20/27/26/17/10 split is a judgment call dressed up in more rigor than it can actually bear — the 27 for training and 26 for employee support are where I'd genuinely put the weight, because the survey uncertainty and rising turnover say the human side is where transitions fail, and the 20 for automation is a scope-level bet I can defend but not prove at the margin. The 17 for data infrastructure and 10 for the innovation lab are the numbers I've been least able to justify with a mechanism, and I've said so out loud rather than pretending otherwise. What I'd want a newcomer to understand is that the real product of our committee wasn't the percentages — it was a record of which numbers are evidence-backed, which are judgment, and which are just residue from a concession I made under pressure, plus one live watch on automation that can actually fire against my own number. If the turnover data comes back bad, the honest move is to reopen the split rather than defend it, and I've committed to that in writing.

My final position is to hold the package at 20/27/26/17/10, with the 20 for automation, 27 for workforce training, 26 for employee support, 17 for the innovation lab, and 10 for data infrastructure — and to be honest that this is judgment, not argued magnitude. The 20 rests on a reversibility argument (weight reversible bets up, irreversible ones down) rather than a real floor, and I've accepted a binding, two-directional watch on that line owned by Ellis, with the consequence firing whichever way it breaks. The 27 and 26 remain unwatched, and I name that as a declined gap rather than an oversight. I won't dress the hold as a verdict on the brief or add new artifacts to make it feel more earned; the round's honest product is the unchanged integers plus the report-back language naming the choice, the confessions, and the blind spot that numbers travel while confessions don't.
